name: Harold Ward
bio: Harold Ward was a Black official of the United Electrical/Farm Equipment workers (UE-FE) and a leader of the 1952 International Harvester strike in Chicago, charged with murder in the death of a strikebreaker in what the National Guardian called a 'new Haymarket.' Held without bail and tried twice, he was ultimately acquitted of both counts by the end of 1952.
charges: Murder of a strikebreaker during the 1952 International Harvester strike — a labor frame-up of a Black union leader.
convicted: No — acquitted of both counts by December 1952.
sentence: Held without bail through two trials; acquitted.

name: Clyde Brown
bio: Clyde Brown was a Black man held two and a half years under a death sentence for rape in Winston-Salem, North Carolina, in a case his defenders called a frame-up — the alleged victim testified she 'didn't remember.' The U.S. Supreme Court granted a hearing in his case in 1952.
charges: Rape — a capital conviction the defense and the Civil Rights Congress called a racial frame-up.
convicted: Convicted and under death sentence; the Supreme Court granted review in 1952.

name: Ocie Jugger
bio: Ocie Jugger was a Black man executed in Louisiana in July 1952 on a rape charge his defenders said was never proved and rested on a confession beaten out of him after his 1948 arrest. He was put to death alongside Paul Washington in a case the Civil Rights Congress condemned as a legal lynching.
charges: Rape — a capital charge the defense called an unproven racial frame-up resting on a coerced confession.

name: Sam Jordan
bio: Sam Jordan was a young Black man facing extradition from Bayonne, New Jersey to a Georgia chain gang over the theft of seed peas — a charge for which his white co-defendants had gone free. The Civil Rights Congress fought to block his return south.
charges: Theft (seed peas) — a Georgia chain-gang sentence his white co-defendants escaped.
convicted: Convicted in Georgia; fought extradition from New Jersey.
sentence: A Georgia chain-gang term; the CRC fought his extradition.

name: Don Martin
bio: Don Martin was a Black U.S. Army private charged with rape and kidnapping at Laguna Beach, California, despite an alibi placing him 300 miles away at Camp Ord. His defenders publicized the case as a racial frame-up.
charges: Rape / kidnapping — a charge the defense met with an alibi 300 miles away, calling it a racial frame-up.

name: Marie Richardson
bio: Marie Richardson was a Black Progressive Party leader in Washington, D.C. convicted in March 1952 of falsely denying Communist Party membership on a Library of Congress job application. Bail was denied and she was given a heavy sentence in what supporters saw as a political frame-up.
charges: False statement — denying Communist Party membership on a federal job application.
sentence: 28 months to 7 years and a $2,000 fine.

name: Olga Viscal Garriga
bio: Olga Viscal Garriga was a young Puerto Rican independence-movement spokeswoman jailed after the 1950 Nationalist uprising. She was sentenced on dozens of contempt counts (about 930 days) along with uprising-related charges, refusing to recognize U.S. jurisdiction over Puerto Rico.
charges: Contempt of court (31 counts) and charges arising from the 1950 Nationalist uprising.

name: Vidal Santiago Diaz
bio: Vidal Santiago Díaz was Pedro Albizu Campos's barber, besieged for hours and shot and wounded by police and National Guardsmen in his San Juan barbershop during the 1950 Puerto Rican Nationalist uprising. Seized wounded and unarmed, he was sentenced to about two years.
charges: Charges arising from the 1950 Nationalist uprising (after an hours-long police siege of his barbershop).

name: Deusdedit Marrero
bio: Deusdedit Marrero was a Puerto Rican Communist and independence figure convicted under Puerto Rico's 'Gag Law' (Law 53) of advocating the overthrow of the insular government. He was held in the Arecibo jail and, supporters reported, denied his mail and reading material.
charges: Puerto Rico 'Gag Law' (Law 53) — advocating the overthrow of the insular government.
sentence: Several years (reported 4–6, up to 6–12); held at Arecibo.

name: Stanley Dale Sydow
bio: Stanley Dale Sydow was a Korean War objector prosecuted in Omaha in 1952 for refusing induction into the Army, mounting a defense grounded in the Nuremberg principles against waging aggressive war. He faced a federal prison term.
charges: Refusing induction into the armed forces (conscientious objection to the Korean War).

name: Fyke Farmer
bio: Fyke Farmer was a war-tax resister who refused to pay federal income tax on the ground that the Korean War was illegal under the Nuremberg principles. The government placed a $4,733 lien on his home.
charges: Refusal to pay federal income tax for war (war-tax resistance test case).
sentence: A $4,733 tax lien on his home.

name: Eugene Moy
bio: Eugene Moy was the editor of the New York China Daily News, a Chinese-American paper sympathetic to the new People's Republic of China, indicted in 1952 on dozens of counts under the Trading With the Enemy Act. The prosecution was widely seen as an attack on the Chinese-American left press.
charges: Trading With the Enemy Act (53 counts) — over the China Daily News's reporting on People's China.
sentence: A prison term and fine (press-freedom prosecution).

name: Albert Wong
bio: Albert Wong was a former managing editor of the New York China Daily News, indicted with editor Eugene Moy in 1952 under the Trading With the Enemy Act over the paper's pro-People's-China stance.
charges: Trading With the Enemy Act — as a former editor of the China Daily News.
sentence: Prosecution under the Trading With the Enemy Act.

name: Jacob Daniel Webster Greene
bio: Jacob Daniel Webster Greene was prosecuted for criminal libel in Harrison County, Indiana for distributing antiwar reprints critical of President Truman and the Korean War. He was first committed to a hospital for the criminally insane for six months 'for observation' — then found sane — and held for trial.
charges: Criminal libel — for distributing antiwar literature critical of Truman and the Korean War.
convicted: Held for trial; first committed to an asylum 'for observation.'
sentence: Six months' psychiatric commitment; awaited trial.
